name: Bedroom temperature (cold room, 65F)
lead: The cold-room habit keeps the bedroom cool, often around 65 F (about 18 C), by lowering the thermostat, opening a window or running a fan. In looksmaxxing and wellness communities it is used for deeper, more continuous sleep, which proponents link to fresher skin, less under-eye darkness, better recovery from training and healthier hormones.

Sleep-hygiene guidance recommends a quiet, very dark and cool sleeping area and says noise, light and uncomfortable temperatures have been shown to disrupt continuous sleep [1]. Dermatology references list fatigue among the factors that make skin look paler and under-eye circles more visible [2], which is the chain from sleep to appearance that communities cite.

Reference sources do not name 65 F as a specific target, and describe evidence for sleep-hygiene advice overall as weak and inconclusive, with a 2021 American Academy of Sleep Medicine review not favouring it as a stand-alone insomnia treatment [1].

chain: Rested-looking skin and eyes, better training recovery
angle.text: People keep the bedroom cool so they sleep without overheating, which they say shows up as brighter skin, fewer dark circles and more energy to train. The appearance benefit runs through sleep quality.

paras: The habit lowers the thermostat or ventilates the room at night. It usually sits alongside other bedroom changes such as darkness, quiet and a consistent bedtime, which sleep-hygiene guidance groups together [1].

Fatigue is one of the factors listed for dark circles, since tiredness makes skin look paler so underlying vessels show more [2]. Proponents of the cold room cite this link when they say better sleep improves how the eyes and skin look.

No studies found for the specific 65 F target or for appearance outcomes. Guidance covering bedroom conditions generally, including temperature, has been evaluated as part of sleep hygiene for insomnia, where results were weak and inconclusive and a 2021 review did not support it as a stand-alone treatment [1]. Work on cold exposure more broadly, such as a clinical trial of physiological responses to mild cold in young men, concerns waking cold exposure rather than sleep [3].

The cold room appears alongside fixed bedtimes, screen limits, no alcohol and cooling bedding as part of a sleep routine. A poster in a T Nation thread describes trying 'all the sleep hygiene stuff (no screens, no alcohol, cold room)' while still waking after a few hours, illustrating that members treat it as one element of a set [4].

lore.intro: In forums the cold room is mentioned as part of a bundle of sleep habits rather than as a stand-alone practice.

claims.claim: A cold room improves sleep, and better sleep improves how you look
claims.believers: Members include 'cold room' among sleep-hygiene steps meant to produce deeper sleep and a more rested appearance [4].
claims.experts: Sleep-hygiene guidance recommends a cool sleeping environment and notes temperature discomfort can disrupt sleep, while rating the overall evidence for the advice as weak [1]. No published study has tested a 65 F bedroom against appearance outcomes.

card.summary: Sleeping in a cool room; recommended in sleep-hygiene advice, but the specific 65 F figure is untested here.
card.note: Sleep hygiene overall has weak evidence as a standalone treatment.

quick.overview:
People keep the bedroom cool, often about 65 F, to sleep better.

Guidance backs a cool sleeping environment generally, but no source reviewed tests a specific temperature or appearance effects.
quick.mechanism: Uncomfortable temperatures can disrupt continuous sleep, so a cooler room is meant to reduce disruption.
quick.risks: No documented risks beyond personal comfort.
